utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Dermot Groome and I'm accompanied by Edward Jeremy and Ms. Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much Mr. Groome. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic, Miodrag Stojanovic, Milos Saljic, and Dan Ivetic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic. Judge Orie is indisposed today. May the record please show that for that reason the Chamber is sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Thank you so much. Before we start with the witnesses for the day, there are a number of procedural issues that the Chamber would like to raise. First of all, as the request for support staff to question witnesses and make submissions in Court. On the 26th of July, 2012, through an informal communication the Defence requested a standing authorisation for two of its members to question witnesses and make submissions in Court. The Chamber initially deferred its decision on this request and notified the Defence of this on the 2nd of August, 2012. On the 7th of August, 2012, the Defence requested authorisation for Mr. Dragan Ivetic to cross-examine four upcoming witnesses, two of whom are scheduled for the first week of court. On 13th of August, 2012, the Chamber granted the request in part allowing Mr. Ivetic to cross-examine witnesses Doyle and Jordan. The second point was that the Prosecution's submissions on adjudicated facts and agreed facts and agreed facts reporting. On the 18th of July, 2012, the Prosecution suggested to refer to adjudicated facts. This Chamber has taken judicial notice of when choosing not to elicit certain evidence from witnesses in the lines on the adjudicated facts. The Defence did not respond to this submission. The Chamber appreciates this proposal from the Prosecution and supports it. Also, on 18th of July, 2012, the Prosecution suggested a procedure to inform the Chamber of agreements or stipulations between the parties. The Defence did not oppose this procedure on the 20th July 2012. The Chamber welcomes the parties' efforts in relation to finding agreement and focusing on disputed matters. In relation to the suggested procedure for notifying the Chamber, the Chamber would prefer that any agreements or stipulations are noted down by the parties and filed on the record. In that way, such agreements or stipulations are traceable, much easier than by searching the transcript for certain words. In that respect, the Chamber also amends its previous instructions to file bimonthly reports on agreed facts and Rule 65 ter (e)(i) admissions. From now on, such reports should be filed whenever there are relevant developments on any agreements between the parties. Item 3. Guidance on tendering public redacted versions of documents. On the 19th of July, 2012, the Prosecution tendered the statement of Witness RM255 as a confidential document as well as a redacted version as a public document. The Chamber mentioned that it would further consider whether such public redacted versions should also form part of the body of the evidence. The Chamber now provides its guidance. In order to avoid duplication of the evidentiary record, the Chamber considers that whenever possible public redacted versions of confidential exhibits should be filed on the record. For 92 ter statements this could be done already in an additional public annex to the respective Rule 92 ter motion. Number 4. Rule 65 ter exhibit lists, missing translations. On the 20th of July, 2012, the Prosecution filed its third motion to amend the Rule 65 ter exhibit list. The Defence responded, and the Chamber also noticed that many of the proposed exhibits do not have an English translation attached in e-court. The Chamber hereby instructs the Prosecution to upload the missing English translations into e-court and to notify the Chamber and the Defence once it has done so. The Chamber further instructs the Prosecution to review the proffered documents so as to ensure that there is no overlap with any of the adjudicated facts of which the Chamber has taken judicial notice and to provide the Chamber with an update on this when giving notification in relation to the missing translations. On the 10th of August, 2012, the Prosecution requested leave to reply to the Defence's response. The Chamber hereby grants the Prosecution's request and considers that attached reply as filed. Item number 5. Prosecution Rule 92 bis motion concerning RM57. On 30th of May, 2012, the Chamber staff requested the Prosecution by means of informal communication to review the 92 bis motion in light of adjudicated facts numbers 346, 353, 426, 447, 867, 877 to 879, 893 to 895, 929, 936, 946, 960, 965 to 966, 972, 974, 982 to 983, 986 to 990, 1002 to 1004, 1006, 1008 to 1020, 1115 and 1117. The Prosecution was instructed to indicate through a formal filing whether it pursues the motion and, if so, how it proposes to deal with possible overlap between adjudicated facts and the Rule 92 bis evidence should the Chamber decide to grant the motion. The Chamber hereby places this informal communication on the record and seeks an update from the Prosecution on the matter. Are you ready to give that update, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'd ask if I could do that after the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of course, you can. Thank you so much. Item 6. Harland MFI P3. During the testimony of Witness Harland, document P3 was MFI'd. P3 is a Prosecution map binder for this case. The Defence objected that the maps contained markings and drawings introducing unproven facts. The Chamber recognises that the markings in P3 are mainly illustrations of the Prosecution's case which need to be proven by evidence. The Chamber is aware of this and will not rely on these markings in making any findings. As a result, the map binder will be treated mainly as a reference. With this explanation the Chamber admits P3 into evidence. Lastly, number 7, Schmitz's MFI's. 65 ter 19814 is a 75-paged document, portions of which the Prosecution and the Defence used with Witness Schmitz in court. On 17th July, 2012, the Chamber instructed the parties to tender only the specific pages they sought to rely on from within 65 ter 19814 for admission. I refer you to transcript pages 940, 958, 1013 to 1014. On the 20th of July, 2012, Mr. Lukic indicated the Defence wanted to raise a purely practical matter concerning 65 ter 19814 and would do so in an informal communication, and that's at transcript 1281. The Prosecution and the Defence sent e-mails on 23rd of July, 2012. The Registrar filed an internal memorandum assigning exhibit numbers to pages of 65 ter 19814 separately uploaded by the Prosecution and Defence pursuant to the Chamber's instructions. P63 to P65 was filed by the Prosecution; and D27 to D37 was filed by the Defence, and all of them were filed marked for identification. As of the 14th of August, 2012, P63 to P65 appear with B/C/S translations in e-court. Mr. Groome, the Chamber would like to know whether, from the Prosecution's point of view, these documents are now ready for admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, they are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you are tendering them accordingly?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Then P63 to P65 are therefore formally admitted into evidence. D27 to D37 do not yet have B/C/S translations. Mr. Lukic, can we expect that the B/C/S translations would be uploaded soon?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Defence has one problem since it cannot ask CLSS for B/C/S translations, so only if you can accept draft translations from the team members we could do that. Otherwise, we have to address the Prosecution to help on this issue as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response, Mr. Groome, to that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be cautious about adopting or agreeing to a change of practice. I would -- I think the more sensible thing at this stage, I would suggest, would be to make an inquiry with CLSS about when they anticipate they will have the translations and then see whether that presents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As I understand Mr. Lukic, he says the Defence cannot approach CLSS for B/C/S translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I have an opportunity to speak with Mr. Lukic over the break and see if there is some accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We will hear from you later. That concludes the procedural issues. May the witness please be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Stewart informs me it may be possible that the Prosecution is already in possession of some translations of the documents that Mr. Lukic is referring to. So when we discuss this over the break it may be that we will be able to provide the Defence with the translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Groome. We'll wait to hear whether you do have them, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if I can make use of the time. The next witness is Aernout van Lynden and he has informed me that he would be assisted if he could have a hard copy of his statement before him to refer to if he is asked questions about it. With the permission of the Court, I have brought an unmarked copy of his statement here, and if the Chamber approves this, I would ask that the usher show this to Mr. Lukic and then it be provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have any objections on this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. May the usher please show the unmarked document to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. van Lynden, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, I am aware that this is not the first time that you have come and testified before the Tribunal. You must be aware with the procedures in our Court here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I hand you over to Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we begin by having you state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: My name is Aernout van Lynden. What do you want my full --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That will suffice, thank you. Now, Mr. van Lynden, is it true that you have previously provided written statements to the Office of the Prosecutor and testified before this Tribunal in a number of other trials in relation to your work as a journalist in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Among those written statements that I've just referred to, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor which you signed on the 16th of March, 2010, before giving evidence in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is also true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that 65 ter 28338 be brought to our screens. It is the statement to which I have just referred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May it please be brought up to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, once the document is on the screen before you, can I ask that you take a look at the first page, in particular, the signature at the bottom of the page and indicate whether you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we go to the last page of the statement which is e-court page 46. And, again, Mr. van Lynden, I would ask you whether you recognise the signature on this page.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do. That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, since giving this statement or signing this statement, have you had an opportunity to read and review it and the associated -- the exhibits associated to it; namely, the video reports that you filed during your time in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I note in paragraph 1 of your statement, it omits to mention that you testified in the Mrksic and Martic cases. Did you, in fact, testify in those two cases?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Apart from that omission, is there any correction or addition you wish to make to your statement?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not at this time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I were to take the time today to ask you questions similar to those that you were asked during the creation of this statement, would you give the same answers in substance?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now that you have taken the solemn declaration, do affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of this statement?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders Mr. van Lynden's statement, 65 ter 28338, pursuant to 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Groome. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. 65 ter 28338 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28338 receives number P66, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave I will now read a short summary of Mr. van Lynden's written evidence. Mr. van Lynden's actual evidence, of course, is the statement itself and will be available to the public. Aernout van Lynden worked as a war correspondent for 23 years. Before becoming a journalist, Mr. van Lynden was a reserve infantry officer in the Dutch marine corps for two years. During such time he commanded a Mortar Platoon. In May 1992, Mr. van Lynden working as a television journalist for British news channel Sky News first arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He spent the majority of his time in Sarajevo until September 1992. After that time, Mr. van Lynden covered other parts of Bosnia but continued to make regular trips to Sarajevo throughout 1993 and 1994. In Sarajevo Mr. van Lynden stayed mainly at the former JNA military hospital, also known as the State Hospital, and later the City Hospital, a building located in central Sarajevo. From the top floor of the hospital, he and his crew had an excellent vantage point over the city. Mr. van Lynden observed the conditions in which the population lived, including the severe lack of food, water, and utilities. He observed the sniping and shelling campaign against the city and the fear that this campaign created within that civilian population. In September and October of 1992, Mr. van Lynden reported from Pale to try and cover the war from the Serb side. Mr. van Lynden met with Radovan Karadzic on a number of occasions during this time. He also interviewed General Mladic in September of 1992. This concludes the summary, Your Honour. Your Honours, unique to this witness is the fact that many of the associated exhibits are news reports depicting events in Sarajevo. It is my intention to work with many of these during my examination of Mr. van Lynden and ask some specific questions regarding them. I will therefore, in observance of the Chamber's expressed preference, will tender these associated exhibits once I have worked with them. At the end of the examination, I will tender a remaining ten exhibits which I will not specifically address during my brief examination here this morning. If that is acceptable to the Chamber, I will proceed with my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, I would like to begin by having you updated your professional biographies. Paragraphs 3 and 5 of your statement summarise your biography as of the time you signed your statement in March 2010. Can I ask you to summarise your professional activities since that time.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In March 2010, I was living in Rome. Due to the death of my wife. I've had to move back to the Netherlands at the beginning of last year, and I am now employed as a staff lecturer at Leiden university college here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what courses do you lecture on?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I give three courses on journalism and three courses on war studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, throughout your statement you referred to various places within Sarajevo. Having lived and worked in Sarajevo for the period you did, were you generally familiar with the city, its neighbourhoods and its greater environs in the period from 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, although not an expert. I did not grow up in the city, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Over the course of your testimony here this morning I will play for the Court several news reports that you submitted to Sky News which were publically broadcast. In preparation for giving evidence about these reports were you asked to verify the accuracy of a Prosecution exhibit which relates stills taken from some of your reports to the locations in which they were made on a panoramic photograph of the Sarajevo skyline?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask that 65 ter 28339 be brought to our screens. Your Honour, given that this is a panoramic photograph and given the limitations of our -- the monitors we have before us, I have taken the liberty of making hard copies of this exhibit. I think it will be more efficient or will facilitate the Chamber's understanding of the witness's evidence. So with the Chamber's permission, I would ask that they be distributed at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May they be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that the witness also be given a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, we will provide you with a hard copy as well but we can now see the electronic on the screen before us. Can I ask you to tell us whether you recognise this exhibit and, if so, what you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: A photograph of Sarajevo taken from the south of the city towards the north and then there are a number of clips from -- or stills from stories that I did in 1992 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now an arrow points from each of these stills to a location within Sarajevo. Do these arrows accurately point to the approximate location of where these stories were filmed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, the stories were filmed from -- largely from the former military hospital. That's the white building slightly to the right of the centre. So some of the other shots are -- for instance, the top shot of the Unis towers burning I am standing on the balcony of the hospital and the Unis towers are behind me. The shot on the right hand at the top that was taken at -- not at the military hospital but on that corner. The -- on the left-hand side at the bottom of the apartment block, again, the cameraman and I were in front of that building. All the other five stills that you have put by -- were taken all -- these are footage shot at the military hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just for my own edification ask, Mr. van Lynden, you're saying at page 14, line 2: The shot object the right hand at the top that was not taken -- not at the military hospital but on that corner. On which corner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The corner is in the centre of town not far from the Bosnian Presidency. It's not very far from the hospital --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to give some permanent feature there to identify that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an extremely dangerous place because it was open to direct sniper fire, and later in the war the Bosnians erected with containers a sort of -- build a kind of wall for civilians to be able to pass by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I go back to my question: Is there a permanent feature from where you took this photograph that you can give to describe the position at which you were when you took the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A feature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. A building or something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, clearly we had our backs to the building so that we were not in the direct line of fire and the people you see running were in the direct line of fire there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does the arrow pointing to the right-hand side of the main picture of the -- indicate the position where you were at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's obviously very rough, given the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you give me a map of Sarajevo I think that I will be able to say what the location was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the purpose of that arrow is to give a general direction of where you were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, when we actually look at the clips when the Chamber looks at the clips, will it be apparent to them the buildings that are in the areas of the clips?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It should be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you referred to the military hospital. Is that -- a white building. Is that the building there is a red square around?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 28339 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We never object to maps, Your Honours, but we would object to this kind of presentation because we still don't know what -- what each of these photographs are. Maybe at the end of this gentleman's testimony we could say more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I thought Mr. van Lynden explained what those various pictures are. There's the parliament, the military hospital, railway yard, apartment blocks, you know, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps it will assist Mr. Lukic, at the bottom of each of the stills is a 65 ter number. That's the 65 ter number of the clip for which the still was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot check now, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not object or I will not protest -- or reserving a decision on this until the conclusion of the witness's evidence. Perhaps Mr. Lukic will be in a better position then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Will it then be marked for identification, Madam Registrar, and be given an number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28339 will receive number P67, MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I now ask that the Court Officer bring to our screens 65 ter -- I'm sorry, P3. This is the map book for Sarajevo. And could I ask that we go directly to e-court page 63. This is a military map of the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, because of the size of this exhibit, it may take a few moments to bring it to our screens. But in paragraphs 76 to 90 of your statement you refer to an interview you conducted with General Mladic in September of 1992. In paragraph 78 of your statement, you refer to a map on which the position marked KAG-1 appeared to you to be the approximate location where you conducted this interview of Mr. Mladic. I can see that we can now see a map on the screen. Is this a portion of the map in which you identified this location?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask for the assistance of the usher. I'm going to ask Mr. van Lynden to mark that location as well as another relevant location on this map. And I believe the Prosecution has been using blue for -- I'm sorry, red, for the marks that we have been asking the witnesses to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, could I ask you to circle the approximate location of where you interviewed Mr. Mladic in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to simply put RM next to that circle to indicate that.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, without making any marks -- other marks for the moment, are you able to see the down-town Sarajevo area on this map?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to circle -- or which parts of the down-town -- which parts of Sarajevo can you see on the map?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: All of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you see the old town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to circle the old town of Sarajevo on this map.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can I ask you to just right "old town" underneath to indicate that.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would ask that this graphic be tendered -- I would tender this graphic into evidence. It is from P3 and it is marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3, as marked by the witness, will receive number P68, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I am finished with that. Thank you, Mr. Usher. Can I now ask that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While this exhibit is being processed, Mr. van Lynden, in paragraphs 31 to 35 of your statement, you say that in the first few days of your -- after your arrival in Sarajevo, you decided to base yourself at the State Hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In those paragraphs you describe the proximity of the building to the confrontation lines as well as the views of the city that you had from my -- from the building. My question is whether you considered the views from the hospital generally expansive and unobstructed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They were. From the -- if we are looking direct from the front of the building we could see the actual confrontation lines. The parliament and behind that you can see the river but that's where the Miljacka river ran and then Grbavica, the area of town held by the Bosnian Serbs. On the -- there was a small balcony on the left and there we could film the old part of Sarajevo and a balcony on the right which gave us a view towards the whole of new Sarajevo, as it was called, Novo Sarajevo. And it was unobstructed. We had a very, very, clear view which is why we chose it to -- as a place really to spend our nights because we could film what was happening in the city if the city came under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was the view generally unobstructed in all directions?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Generally. The danger was at the front of the building that we knew that we were therefore visible, possibly visible, to those on the southern hills of Sarajevo who were actually shooting at the city. So those were very dangerous positions. Most of the windows at the front of the building had been broken because the hospital itself had come under fairly sustained fire since the fighting in Sarajevo began.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we now have 65 ter 10467 on the screen before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, I'd ask you to now take a look at the photograph which should be on the screen before you and ask you do you recognise what is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. This is the part of the former military hospital in which we stayed on the top floor, Your Honours. The hospital is bigger than that. There are other buildings as well. As you can see in the photograph, the building has been fairly -- been hit fairly regularly and fairly badly. Other parts of the building -- of the hospital buildings were also struck by artillery fire and by -- generally what we would consider heavy machine-gun fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does this photograph fairly and accurately depict the State Hospital and its condition as you recall it from your time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. The situation actually got worse, because according to me this is a photograph from 1992 and the hospital was hit after that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your last member of this hospital is that it had sustained additional damage to what we can see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The particular side of the building that we are looking at in this photograph, are you able to tell us in which direction it is facing? What is the compass point that it is facing?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The facade of the building that we are seeing is facing south.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So someone looking out one of the windows that we can see here would be looking in a southerly direction?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraph 35 of your written evidence, you state that the State Hospital was targeted by gun-fire and on one occasion even a tank shell. Based on your experience while being stationed there, or using this facility, how often was the State Hospital targeted?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Most of the damage had been done prior to my arrival there, but while we were there, it was repeatedly hit. Specifically in those days of early June, which you will come to, when we filmed Sarajevo being shelled, it was hit every single night. And we were aware that it was a dangerous position. On the other hand, if a building is going to be targeted, people will generally aim for the middle rather than the top, and therefore I felt actually relatively safe being on the top floor, strange as that may sound to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in addition to this hospital being in existence prior to the war, can you recall when you first saw the emblem of the Red Cross draped across its facade as we can see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I remember that as -- either at the end of June or the beginning of July 1992. It may have been there before, but I do not recall it when I first arrived in Sarajevo in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your statement and in your evidence a few moments ago you referred to balconies from which much of the filming was done. Are we able to see those balconies in this particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, we are not. They are very narrow balconies, probably not even a metre wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to use this photograph to assist the Chamber in understanding where those balconies where?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, they were right on the outside of the building. So here -- well, I would say was the right-hand side of the building and here the left had a balcony and then the opposite side of the building also had one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So they are on the sides of the building --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- that we cannot see but are adjacent to the side that we can see?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 10467 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10467 receives number P69, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, in paragraphs 21 to 26 of your statement you describe your observations on civilian life in Sarajevo. In particular, in paragraph 25, you state: "Using a combination of physical and psychological terror enabled the Serbs to turn, alter the heat on Sarajevo as the political military situation demanded." Can you briefly describe what you meant by this?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Because of their command of the heights around Sarajevo which is an elongated city lying by the river-bed in the valley, because of that, if they wished to, at any moment, any part of the city could be shelled, and various parts of the city, they could literally snipe down the streets. That is one form of -- yeah, I would say psychological terror. The other was that this was a city besieged and therefore there wasn't running water, there was no electricity and there were no ready food supplies. Already by the time I arrived there in May 1992, no shops existed anymore. So they had control also of the basic needs of the civilian population. Once the United Nations started getting food into the city much of the food came by air into Sarajevo airport but that supply could be stopped very easily by simply firing a few shots at the incoming aircraft. And then the whole airlift would be stopped for days, sometimes for weeks. So it was very easy, as I said, to turn on the heat on Sarajevo as the political and military situation demanded. For the civilian position living there for almost four years of siege it was really a constant that they were under psychological pressure, sometimes of a very extreme nature, certainly for those who had small or adolescent children.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, paragraph 44 of your statement refers to a story that you filed on the situation in Sarajevo in May of 1992. I'm going to now play that clip and I will have some questions for you afterward. In order to save time, I will ask Ms. Stewart to play the clip from the beginning until 28.5 seconds. I will rely on the clip's association to the statement to establish the foundation for admission of the remainder of the clip. Or should the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the document number?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 22460A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, of course, if the Chamber would wish to view the entire clip here in Court we are prepared to play that. For the convenience of all parties, the English and B/C/S transcript of this video and all other videos that I will show today are available in e-court under the same 65 ter number of the clip, and the booths have been provided transcripts of these clips that will be used this morning. Before playing the clip, I will ask Ms. Stewart to stop on a graphic that appears before the clip actually commences. Variations of this graphic appear on most of the clips I will use today. I will ask Mr. van Lynden to explain the meaning of this graphic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, what we can see now on our screens is a graphic. Can I ask you to help decipher the information that's provided in this graphic.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is what we call a clock. As you can see then a clock only in terms of seconds that is put or was put before everything single video story before it went on air in an actual news broadcast. It also helps the producers of a programme to see to it that they go at precisely the right moment that you don't have black before the story starts. Apart from that, there is a date of when it first went out, PGM at 1800, what kind of day it was, a Monday, and then the date, the 1st of June, 1992. That is done for library purposes so that a story of that nature can be found, if needed, in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And PGM stands for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So would I be correct in saying that the clip we are about to see was first aired on Sky News on the 1st of June in the 6.00 news?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And does this necessarily reflect the precise day on which the video in the report was shot?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. This, Your Honours, I maybe need to explain that when I was first sent to Sarajevo in May 1992, a decision had been taken by management of Sky News in London that the editing facilities and the picture editor, the person who gets the pictures and then puts them in an order for them to be broadcast and the satellite uplink with which the story was, as we call it, fed from Bosnia into London, that they should remain in Pale and not go with me into Sarajevo. That forced me during that initial period on every day that I had a story to actually cross the lines across the Bosnian -- into the Bosnian Serb lines from Sarajevo into the suburb of Ilidza where a local producer would meet us and he would then take the tapes and drive them to Pale while we crossed back over into Sarajevo again. It was a complex procedure that we didn't, thankfully, repeat later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As a rule, what was the approximate time period between the time that you and your cameramen would capture an image, a story, and that it would be broadcast by Sky News?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It usually meant that the filming had been done the day before, possibly the same morning, but not after that, because after that, we would be handing over the tape in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with that introduction I would now ask Ms. Stewart to play the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "In Sarajevo the cross-roads can be lethal, need to be taken at speed. They and the avenues that cut across the city offer the Serb gunners in the hills above with open lines of fire. Prime targets which the old and the infirm are forced to accept as the new uncomfortable realities of life. As the people of Sarajevo ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, is that your voice that we hear during the story?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It is, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who wrote the text that you speak?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this the first story that you filed after your arrival in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The scenes on that video-clip were they exceptional of your experience in Sarajevo during your time there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not at all. They were absolutely normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the clip you refer to the Serb gunners in the hills above. How did you know they were Serb gunners in those hills?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, we had driven through those hills and passed Serb positions in those hills in coming to Sarajevo and coming into Sarajevo, because we drove across Mount Trebevic to the Lukavica barracks and then across Sarajevo airport to be able to enter the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 22460A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Okay. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22460A is becomes Exhibit P70, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I inquire when the Chamber would like to take the first break so I can be mindful of the clips and where best to pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We didn't change the scheduling and this would be an opportune time to take a break, a 20-minute break. We take one-hour sessions and break for 20 minutes at each time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. van Lynden, we will take a break of 20 minutes. We will come back at 20 past 10.00. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I see Mr. Mladic is standing on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's his glasses. He wants to leave as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, he will leave just now in a moment. May he please take a seat. Do sit down, please, Mr. Mladic. Thank you. Court adjourned. We come back at 20 past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Groome. I beg your pardon. May the witness please be brought into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, generally speaking, this morning I will be showing your reports in a chronological order but the next clip that I want to show you is not in chronological order but is from a report you filed in December 1992. Now, with respect to the sniping of civilians in paragraph 49 of your statement, you say that this became so common that unless there were unusual or aggravating features to the sniping incident, it was really not newsworthy. I would also refer the Chamber to adjudicated fact 2018, which provides: "Between September 1992 and August 1994, civilians were shot at almost every day." In reliance on this, I will not explore the sniping of civilians, the evidence which you can provide on this, but I would refer you to paragraph 122 and 127 of your statement where you refer to an attack on a civilian apartment block in the context of the battle of Otes in December 1992. I'd like to play a clip of your story about that attack referenced in paragraph 126 and then ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution will now play video-clip 65 ter 22461A. I would ask Ms. Stewart to begin to play from 1 minute, 35 seconds and play until 2 minutes, 41 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Words mirrored by the reality in the city. Serb incendiary rounds, setting a string of flats ablaze in one apartment block. A resident watches, distraught. His home and belongings gone. Seconds later, a further burst of incendiary rounds crash into the building or bounce off the wall into the street below. Wanted arson on a purely civilian target. As ever, Sarajevo's remarkable firemen fight back. Getting their hoses to the flames for once unhampered by a cut in the water supply. But for the fire chief, the water is not the main concern. His engines are running out of fuel, and he tells us he won't be able to cope with another fire this day. "... shelling here in the centre of Sarajevo again on the line. The initial efforts in Bosnia cease-fires and political talks have led nowhere and won't until the western world proves it has a true commitment to ending this war. "Aernout van Lynden, Sky News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, my first question to you is: Is this one of the reports which is indicated, the location of, is indicated in that panoramic photo display which is now P67, marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the clip we saw small red objects striking the apartment block one of which bounces back and over the camera. Do you know what these were?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: These were incendiary rounds. For me that was relatively novel, Your Honours. I served in the Dutch marine corps and within NATO we do not have incendiary rounds fired by guns, but the Yugoslav Army did have these and that is what is being used on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 122 of your statement, "The fire originated --" I believe you mean gun-fire or sniper fire: "The fire originated from the Bosnian Serb side of the confrontation lines." How were you able to tell this?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: A, where the fire was coming from; B for confirmation. After we left that incident, we went to the UN headquarters and spoke to officers there and asked them to verify some of the information that we had got at the scene itself. The direction of where the fire was from and, secondly, whether that building which was a civilian flat building had been used for military purposes by the Bosnians which could have caused this firing. The UN officers confirmed to us that the fire had originated from Bosnian Serb positions and they also confirmed that the people living in this building had told us, that that building had not been used by the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you yourself were there. Did you see anything that would have indicated otherwise to you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, at this time, the Prosecution tenders 22461A into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 22461A is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 22461A becomes Exhibit P71, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, I am now going to return to the period of June 1992 and focus on four of your reports, each of which deal with the sustained attack across the entire expanse of Sarajevo on or shortly after the 6th of June, 1992. Your Honours, the precise dates of these reports is important as they relate to the crimes charged in the indictment in schedule G2 which reads: "A massive bombardment of the city was carried out with a variety of artillery fired from positions all around the city. Civilian targets were damaged and destroyed and a number of civilians were killed and wounded from on or about the 6th of June 1992." I will play an extract of each of these four reports and I will ask Ms. Stewart to pause at the start of each clip. And the first question I will ask you with respect to each clip is to tell the Chamber with as much precision as possible when the video that we are about to see was recorded. And if we could begin with 65 ter 22460C.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Dusk in Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, we do not have the benefit of the graphic in this particular one. Are you able from your own independent recollection to tell us when this was ...

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: According to me, this story was filmed before the Marsal Tito barracks were evacuated at the beginning of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we please continue with the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Amongst the city's ancient minarets the rockets fall, heralding another night of heavy shelling. For the next six hours there is no letup. Eerily lit up by flares, the city is hit from every side, by practically every imaginable projectile. Long lines of heavy machine-gun fire gliding across the roofs, exploding against their targets. Heavy shells slamming into buildings, within seconds engulfing them in flames. A mass of crazy sparks lighting the brow of one hill from a quick fire volley of mortar bombs. "This is a scene of wholesale devastation of a city being obliterated while the world watches, but does nothing."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Next I would like to play the report referred to in paragraph 55 of your statement which refers to the shelling of the Marsal Tito barracks. And this is 65 ter 22460D.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, we do have the benefit of the graphic here so could I ask you, using this as a reminder to you, when was the video footage that we are about to see actually recorded?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is the date that you see in front of you, Your Honours, is of the actual broadcast of the story for the first time, so at 7.00 English time on the 6th of June, 1992. Most of the footage would have been shot the previous evening and during that night in Sarajevo, and we would have driven this story as I had already explained across the lines to Ilidza on earlier in the afternoon of the 6th of June. But much of the footage would have been actually filmed on the 5th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you -- you've just testified that it would -- that -- it would have been filmed the previous evening and during that night?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that the night from the 5th of June to 6th of June?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we now see the clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And when you say "English time," can we accept that all of your times here are English times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Just hours after the evacuation of the troops from the Marsal Tito barracks, it becomes the night's prime target. The shells land long, around Sarajevo's railway yard. But inside the vast army complex those still looking for loot get the message and run. "Not long after, the gunners in the hills above the Bosnian capital find their range, the barracks explodes in flames. The barracks form the principal target, yet no district escapes. From the dark, the rockets streak down, for a moment illuminating Sarajevo's ancient centre before reducing it to further rubble. "They come in ones, in twos, in threes, and it sounds as if the city is crying."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we return to the 28th second of that video and pause on the frame that we see in that time slot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, on the screen before you now is the frame that we see at 28 seconds. Can I ask you to describe what we are looking at?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: These are the mountains overlooking Sarajevo to -- to the east of the city and we -- what we are seeing here - it's not very clear now in the still - is -- well, I think at the time I described as rocket fire emanating from an artillery position on the brow of that hill, mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to actually visit where you believe that the fire that we see here originated from?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I visited a position, whether it is precisely this same one, I cannot say. But a position to the east of Sarajevo, at the top of a mountain, overlooking the city, when I was taken there in September 1992 by the defendant to conduct an interview with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that's Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now play the third clip in the sequence of reports which you returned to in paragraph 59 of your statement, and that is 65 ter 22460E.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now again, Mr. van Lynden, we've paused at the first frame, the graphic. Can you tell us your best recollection of when the film we are about to see was recorded?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The first shots that you see were filmed on the late afternoon of the 6th of June and then during the night from the 6th to the 7th of June with some of the last pictures taken in the early morning on the 7th of June, before, as usual, we drove the tapes to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we now play the entire clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "It was the symbol of modern Sarajevo, now of its destruction. Flames tear across the floors and up into the higher storeys. Showering debris onto the streets at the heart of the Bosnian capital. The disintegration of one of the city's Unis towers reflected in the broken windows of its twin. "300 metres on across the road, the parliament of this newly independent state is also struck. It doesn't burn, but the near Marsal Tito barracks do. Since its evacuation, two days earlier, it has been systematically destroyed. "Every night in Sarajevo, you think it can't get worse, but it does. Making a mockery of the attempts of mediators to bring peace to the city, which is enfolded in war. "Less than 24 hours earlier, the Serb commanders have put their signatures on yet another agreement, affirming a truce, never adhered to, and their readiness to reopen the airport. Now the Serb gunners in the hills show where their true commitment lies. Under a sickle moon, the city rocks to the explosions. Lit up by fire, and a mass of glowing sparks adrift across its roofs. "With daylight we find the intensive-care wards of the city's central hospital packed with amputees in pain. Some will live but the doctors are resigned to this girl's death. Not far from where she lies do others that have gone before. A place of haphazard death, some covered, some not, where maggots crawl the floors. A little house of Bosnian horror. "Aernout van Lynden, Sky News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, I'd like to now play the fourth and final clip of your reports first aired in the beginning of June 1992. Could I ask that we begin to look at 22460F, and, again, if we pause at the graphic. And again, Mr. van Lynden, could you tell us your best recollection as to when the video we are about to see was actually recorded?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This one is slightly different to the ones that have gone before, Your Honours, because on the 8th of June while we did go -- actually get to Ilidza to deliver the tapes, the producer from Pale didn't make it. So this was only handed over on the 9th. Therefore, this was filmed on the night of the 7th and on the 8th, as far as I recollect, and not on the 9th itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we now play the entire clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Sarajevo's burning, in its heart and in its suburbs. Suddenly on Sunday night, the whole city becoming the target. No district spared. All shaking as every ten seconds the rockets, shells and mortars land. The fire so heavy, so incessant, that the deadly streams of light criss-cross each other. "By early Monday morning, the inundation of the hospitals begins. For the doctors and the nurses of the city's former military hospital, already up throughout the night, the beginning of a dark, grim day, the like of which they've never known. Trained fingers, which for 24 hours which will work without respite. To stem blood, extract jagged metal, preserve life. But so many casualties of war, so many distorted faces and torn limbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, I would like to ask you some follow-up questions about the sequence of the four reports that we have seen from the 5th, 6th, 7th and 8th of June. First, a general question relating to all four videos. Where was this footage filmed from?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: All the shelling that you saw was filmed from the top floor of the former military hospital. Of course, there was some footage in one story from the Kosevo academic hospital where you saw the wounded and the dead. This last shot here is also at the Kosevo and there were shots lower down at the casualty department of the military hospital. But all the footage of the buildings burning and of Sarajevo being shelled, those were all filmed from the top floor of the former military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the second video-clip from the 5th and 6th of June, you referred to "the gunners in the hills above the Bosnian capital." Do you know what side those gunners were associated with and how?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Those -- those -- those were the gunners of the Bosnian Serbs. They were the ones with the artillery and with those positions in the hills surrounding the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the same footage of the 5th and 6th of June, you describe what seems to be different types of shelling. In respect to the shell of the Marsal Tito barracks you observe that initially "the shells land long around Sarajevo's railway yard." Shortly afterwards, you describe how the gunners in the hills above Sarajevo find their range. Could you describe in a bit more detail what you meant by this and what you observed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: My personal experience as someone who was trained in the use of mortars and my experience with various artillery units prior to the war in Yugoslavia specifically during the first Gulf War when I was with the American and British forces in Saudi Arabia and was explained the use of artillery by trained artillery officers is that they are given a certain target to fire at and usually the shells either ran long or too short. There are usually spotters or observers who will then try to correct their fire; either the shells have to be fired further or brought in. And it usually takes a minimum of three shells to land before they are spot on their target. This is what I meant by the shells land long on Sarajevo railway yard. Those were shells that were fired too far just over the Marsal Tito barracks. Later they clearly found their range. They brought the shells in and then they were clearly fired at the Marsal Tito barracks that had been evacuated by the Bosnian Serb army and where there was still military equipment lying and it was clearly that that was one target that they wanted to hit and destroy. It is a very large complex dating from the Austro-Hungarian period, 19th century buildings, and they clearly found target and remained on that target. But separate to that, there was shelling right across the city in a quite different kind of one or two shells landing in one district or another district. It was completely unpredictable. For a cameraman it is very, very complicated to film this kind of shelling. If it is sustained on one target then the cameraman can do so. But now it was all over the place. That we were able to capture so much on camera is an indication of just how heavy the fire was during those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 55 of your statement, near the bottom of page 14 in the original you refer to -- you make the following statement: "Simultaneously, I saw fire raining down all over Sarajevo. It was not in the same concentrated manner as the fire directed at the Marsal Tito barracks. It was just shell fire directed at the city with no apparent military purpose." Is this the other type of shelling that you've just referred to during your evidence.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Artillery when it is used for military purposes will take one target and have sustained fire on that target; either to keep opponents from doing an attack or to sustain a military force in doing an attack of their own, or in the case of, for instance, the Marsal Tito barracks because the Bosnian Serbs believed that within those barracks there was military hardware that could be of use to their enemies and therefore they wanted to destroy it. But what we saw in the rest of the city was one or two shells landing completely all over the place and I said just rained down because it came from the skies, and it felt almost as if it was raining shells. But as I said, all over the city and that cannot have had a direct military purpose apart from to bring terror to the lives of everyone living in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the footage of the 6th and 7th of June which features the burning of the Unis towers identified as 22460E for our purposes at the moment, in your statement at paragraph 59 you state that you did not see any outgoing fire from the building. Did you have an opportunity to visit this building and can you tell us what, if any, observations you made about whether there was military activity in the building at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I did visit the building before -- before the evacuation of the Marsal Tito barracks. The Unis towers, if we walked up them, we could look directly into the main square inside the Marsal Tito barracks. However, it was a new building. We couldn't open any windows. It was all centrally air-conditioned. We looked, we asked, I looked then for spent cartridges as an indication whether a building has or has not been used for military purposes and I did not find that, and I did not see that the building had been used for military purposes. I only went into one of the towers, I have to say here, but I didn't see any fire ever emanating from those buildings while we were at the military hospital, nor did I see the military there in any form.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is your best recollection of the date on which you made this visit to one of the towers?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This was just prior to the evacuation of the Marsal Tito barracks. So it would have been on the 2nd and 3rd, 4th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, to those of us who observed these clips, it appears that there are quite a few shells that your cameraman was able to capture. Can I ask you to characterise the relative amount of shells that were captured, depicted here, compared to your own personal observations being in Sarajevo during this period?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, as I already explained, it's -- filming shelling is very, very difficult. What one gets is you get the first initial blast and you see smoke rising, so you start pointing your camera in that direction. One of our problems during those days in Sarajevo was that the next shell might land on the opposite side of the building and we were often running from one balcony on one side of the building to the balcony on the other side of the balcony to try and capture all of the shelling that was going on. So it was very, very difficult. It was almost continuous during those nights, but we did -- that so much was filmed by the cameraman is an indication of just how heavy the shelling was, as I already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, the Prosecution tenders into evidence the four clips we have just viewed. They are 65 ter 22460C, 22460D, 22460E, and 22460F.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Madam Registrar, the four clips are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number respectively.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 22460C become Exhibit P72; 2240 -- 22460D becomes Exhibit P73; 22460E becomes Exhibit P74; and 22460F becomes -- oh, it's not admitted. Is -- yeah?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, it is here.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 22460F becomes Exhibit P75, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, I'd like to now focus your attention on your meeting with General Ratko Mladic in the hills to the east of Sarajevo in September 1992 which you describe in paragraphs 76 to 90 of your statement. I'd first like to play the clip of -- or the news report that you filed with respect to this. And could I now ask that we play 65 ter 22457B.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We can go directly to playing the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Reporter: He is the scourge of Sarajevo, the chief warrior of the Serbs. He is called Ratko Mladic approximately. Ratko means warrior and this square jawed Serb general has lived up to the name. Commander always on the move, the visit to one of the mountain's chalets where the Serbs of Bosnia have established their separatist government is but a fleeting one. In a short briefing, the Commander-in-Chief speaks only of attacks on his forces, never of offences by them. And as if to prove the point he gives us a rare chance to accompany him to front line artillery positions where the UN observers are conspicuous by their absence. High up on the wind swept hills, the 100-millimetres guns are dug deep into the rocks directly overlooking Sarajevo. An overwhelming position of strength which is obviously to the general's satisfaction. As he says, he holds the city in his palm and many of the buildings in the haze below they are testimony to that power. Yet General Mladic's is quite unrepentant. He is man who has no doubts, only a total assurance that he is right, the world wrong, and that his people have been slandered "Ratko Mladic/interpreter: I hope the UN Security Council first takes measures to understand that we Serbs are a reality in this world, no some sort of extraterrestrials and that we have the right to defend ourselves "Reporter: Nearby, more positions are being dug in the general's eyes the world may deny his people their rights but that's not going to stop him. "Ratko Mladic/interpreter: We have to fight as long as we continue to exist to defend ourselves. There is no other way and we are prepared for a long war. "Reporter: Far away from the battle field, the UN is preparing a resolution on war crimes. It leaves Ratko Mladic quite unmoved."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, Mr. Mladic is giving a sign to stop. I'm not quite sure what he wants to say. Can somebody please from your team hear what he is going to say. And speak softly, Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic, Mr. Mladic, Mr. Mladic, speak slowly and speak softly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic. Speak softly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, Mr. Mladic, I am going to stop you there. You can talk to your team during the break. I thought you had something to say about what is happening here. Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask that we un-pause the clip and watch till it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, can you please keep quiet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "R: ... war crimes. It leaves Ratko Mladic quite unmoved. "Ratko Mladic/interpreter: I am not bothered at all. I did not take part in any crimes. I have only defended my people. "R: With that, the general departs to inspect other front lines in a war neither he nor his officers believe will end any time soon. "Aernout van Lynden, Sky News, on the front lines outside Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we return to the 31st second on this clip and pause and that frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, we are now at 31 seconds. Can I ask you to identify the people that are depicted in the frame going from left to right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm the figure on the left. Mr. Mladic is the figure in uniform in the middle. And, on the right is my field producer, Zoran Kusevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we now go to 1 minute, 13 seconds, and hold on that frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now that we are at that point in the report, are you visible in this frame as well?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm the figure on the left. Next to me is Zoran Kusevac, my field producer and interpreter, and then there are three military officers of the Bosnian Serbs, within the middle, Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now ask that we go to 53 seconds in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome and witness, could you please pause between question and answer because some parts of your answers are not recorded properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, we are now at 53 seconds, can I ask you to describe what we see in this frame?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is Mr. Mladic looking through binoculars at the city of Sarajevo which was directly below this artillery position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where is this artillery position in relation to the picnic bench where we see you, Mr. Mladic, and others having a conversation?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The picnic bench was at that location, at the artillery position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And so that the record is clear, is this a different location from the one we saw at 31 seconds where you are looking at a map in an office?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We originally met Mr. Mladic in Pale, and in an office he gave us a briefing of the map, which is what you saw at 31 seconds. He then, somewhat to our own surprise, drove us to this artillery position overlooking Sarajevo from the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in your report you refer to "many of the buildings in the haze below." It is not clear because of the quality of the video what could be observed from this position. Can I ask you to describe what could you see from that position while you were there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if tapes are copied all the time, then the quality diminishes and that is what has happened on this occasion on the tape that the Tribunal holds. But in the original footage you could actually, through the haze, make out the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And which portion of the city was visible, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I mean, really, the whole city, elongated in front of us from the east all the way to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the clip you describe General Mladic indicating to you that he holdings Sarajevo "in his palm." Can I ask you to explain to the Chamber the context in which this occurred and to describe in detail precisely what happened when Mr. Mladic indicated this to you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: When we got to the position, if you do a television story of this nature, you need to get some shots of the people walking around without us in it. And so General Mladic met his officers there and various other people, other soldiers, looked around, and we filmed that, including him looking through the binoculars at Sarajevo. But at a certain moment he asked us to come closer and pointing at the city, gave -- did this, and said, and this was translated to me by my field producer, I hold the city in the palm of my hand. Or words of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to describe what you've just gestured here in court and ask you whether I've probably characterised what you have done. With your right hand, you pointed in front of you at something, and then with that same right hand with the index finger extended you pointed into the cupped palm of your left hand. Is that your best recollection of what Mr. Mladic did?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is my recollection, yes. It made an impression on us. I used it in the story. It wasn't filmed because the cameraman was trying to keep us out of the picture, if -- if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did you understand General Mladic to be conveying to you with this statement and this gesture?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That he did, indeed, hold the power over Sarajevo. That he held all the high ground. I imagine -- we hadn't -- we had requested an interview with Mr. Mladic, but we hadn't requested an interview at an artillery position. We hadn't even been requested to be taken to an artillery position. He took us there. And I think - but this is my reading of the situation - that he was trying to prove to the world but also to his opponents inside Sarajevo: I hold all the commanding positions. I hold the power over you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you see Mladic after your report was aired by Sky News?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I did. A few days later, by chance, we were still working on the Bosnian Serb side, and we encountered each other on the road. He stopped. He got out of the car. We were a little weary because of my opening line to the story, "He is the scourge of Sarajevo." This had been criticised within Pale by certain Bosnian Serbs who felt that I was denigrating their commanding officer. When he came out of the car, however, his first words were, pointing at himself - again this was translated to me by my field producer - I'm the scourge of Sarajevo. And he said it with a smile and was clearly not displeased with the story you have just seen and indeed invited us to lunch at the military position where he was driving to inspect.
