We did indeed accompany him and have lunch there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And over the course of the lunch, did he make any reference to your report or this report?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We talked about it initially, but that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is your recollection of any comment he may have made with respect to that report?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, as far as I'm aware, he had nothing bad to say about the report. Thought was fair. We had let him speak ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution tenders 22457B into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 22457B is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 22457B becomes Exhibit P76, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, in paragraph 88 of your statement, you mentioned that away from the camera you asked General Mladic for permission to visit Bosnian Serb positions around Sarajevo. General Mladic granted you that permission and provided you with an escort of two military policemen. Paragraphs 87 to 112 of your statement describe your tour of these positions, specifically Trebevic, Grbavica, Hrasno, and the area of Sarajevo referred to as the Jewish cemetery. In those paragraphs, you describe in detail your observations. Therefore, I don't propose to ask you any further questions here. Do you know -- the question I do have for you is: Do you know if Mladic was the person who made the arrangements for you to have the military police escort?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Prior to returning to Pale in September 1992, we had been in Pale, and on each occasion that we had tried to work out of Pale on the Bosnian Serb side, we found that within half an hour or so of leaving Pale we would be arrested or detained at a military check-point and finally sent back to Pale again and that we weren't able to work. So I held a number of meetings with Radovan Karadzic, the Bosnian Serb political leader, both at that time and also during the London Conference in August 1992 and finally again at the Intercon hotel in Belgrade in September 1992. And what I requested from him is that we be given some kind of an escort so that we would actually be able to work and film. And Mr. Karadzic agreed. When we got to Pale, we met him. In the end, he provided us also with a letter explaining who we were and that we should be allowed to film. This letter was not signed by him, nor by Mr. Mladic. It was signed by Mr. Krajisnik, who was the Speaker of the Bosnian Serb parliament. And then we were given two military policemen. Now, whether Mr. Karadzic organised that or Mr. Mladic, that I wasn't told. But those two military policemen then accompanied us on any trip we made outside of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now play one of your reports from this -- these visits that you made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we now play 65 ter 22457D and could I ask Ms. Stewart to please begin plying this clip at 35 seconds and play until the end of the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Reporter: The no man's land that's given the area its name is the Jewish cemetery. Across the jumble of graves, new and old, some of the fiercest battles have been fought. The string of little villas lining the cemetery have been turned into bunkers. Sittings room walls roughly redecorated with lines of logs, although some of the defences are more imaginative. Bathroom mirrors, subtly deployed, to allow one guard to view all angles. Of late, the tanks against the Serb lines in this sector have diminished, leaving the battalion commander exuding confidence. "Unidentified officer: We're ready for a long struggle, but we believe we will only spend a short time in these positions. Either they will have to accept peace, or there will be an all-out war in which we will try to achieve victory in a very short time. "Reporter: The major's confidence is understandable. Unlike his opponents, he doesn't face a lack of logistical support made worse by siege. And if he is ordered to attack, he will do so from a commanding position, so commanding that in the streets below, few dare to move. "Aernout van Lynden, Sky News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we return to the 41st second of this clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, we can now see that frame. Can I ask you to describe what we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We're looking at grave stones in what is called -- or what was called the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And from where this is recorded? Where is the cameraman?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In a Bosnian Serb military position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we now go to 1 minute, 37 seconds. And, again, we are now at 1 minute, 37 seconds. Can you tell us what we see in this image?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is a shot of Sarajevo. The buildings we see are north of the river. It's taken from the south from, again, Bosnian Serb military positions, and it shows how, from those positions, you can look straight down the streets of certain parts of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Based on your work in Sarajevo, are you aware of any sniping instances that occurred in the area that is depicted in or near this location?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, there were incidents often there. And I think -- I'm not -- sorry, you can't quite see, but I think that the road has been sort of blocked off by buses or trucks so that civilians can pass unnoticed behind them in the road just by this church.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that maybe, perhaps with the assistance of the usher, if we could ... Your Honour, I'm informed that we would be unable to have the witness make a mark on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to describe, perhaps in a bit greater detail, the feature that you are referring to now. We are unable to have you draw a circle around it for technical reasons.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm referring to, you see the road which is next to it, lying next to the church, the land posts and then there is a white vehicle, another vehicle, a greenish vehicle to its -- to the left and that is blocking off that street so that civilians could pass behind that, and obviously not come under sniper fire from a position from where this was actually filmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during your visits to these locations that we see depicted in reporting, was there any gun-fire emanating out from the positions?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not when we were in -- by the Jewish cemetery, or that we actually filmed when we were in Grbavica, although we heard shots fired and we thought it was from the same building, but when we were taken higher up, Hrasno, there, we actually saw machine-gun fire and filmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 22457D into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can -- Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic, if have you talk to your team, can you talk softly so that we don't have to hear you. Okay. Fair enough. We understand that. Now, you don't have to take three minutes for the Court to stop. Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic. The Court is talking. We understand your request. Just hold it. 22457D is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 22457D becomes P76, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you sure it's 76, Madam Registrar, not 77? 22457B was 76, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. It's Exhibit P77, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Mladic is indicating a request that we stop. It's three minutes before stopping time. Would that be a convenient point for you, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break then, and we will come back at 20 to 12.00. Court adjourned -- before we adjourn, Mr. van Lynden, you may stand down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, how much longer you are you still going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think a little bit more than five minutes, Your Honour. I just have a few more questions now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at 20 to 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be brought into court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, I want to conclude my examination with -- ask a few additional questions about the videos or the reports in general, and perhaps I'm stating something very obvious. But am I correct in saying that the video that was ultimately shown as part of Sky News broadcast was but a portion of all of the video that was recorded by you and your cameraman?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Absolutely. It always is. By definition, any television news report, the usual way we see it is about one minute that makes air, you have 20 to 30 minutes have actually been filmed. It's always edited down. So there is much more material than that is -- that is actually used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Earlier today you described the challenges of trying to record on video shelling that occurred in many different locations at the same time. Were there ever occasions when your cameraman kept the camera on for a prolonged period of time to capture what was happening over the skies of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, there were moments. I mean, he was filming, not me, but I saw the footage afterwards. If the cameraman felt that there was one particular spot that was going to keep on being hit, he would just keep recording on that. But cameramen are taught, certainly television news cameramen are taught, that they have to try to get different shots because it has to be edited and if you have one shot, you can't edit that. So it would never really go much longer than a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this raw footage, do you believe that you still have some possession or have possession of some of the footage that was shot over Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. A tape was made of a sort of compilation of the raw footage of the shelling of Sarajevo in June 1992, and I do, amongst my possessions, have - or had at least - a VHS copy of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would viewing such a video give the viewer a sense of what it would be like to have stood on a rooftop in Sarajevo and observe the shelling on the nights that this footage was created?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We were not on a rooftop.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I mean, from a vantage point?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, under Rule 98 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Chamber can direct the production of evidence. Should the Chamber come to a view that having such raw footage would assist them, would you be willing to search among your belongings for this footage?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, when was the last time you saw Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe that encounter for us, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The encounter took place after what is known as the first market bombing in Sarajevo, in February 1994. I had, at that time -- I wasn't based in Sarajevo; I was based in Central Bosnia. And I then moved to Pale, to the Bosnian Serb headquarters, and a team from Belgrade with our Belgrade bureau chief and a Belgrade cameraman came -- came down from Belgrade to Pale and met me there. A separate team from Sky News went into Sarajevo. We -- the very first day I met with Mr. Karadzic who was not particularly pleased to see me but did give me -- grant me an interview and we stayed there for a couple of weeks. There was a NATO, for the first time, a NATO ultimatum to the Bosnian Serb to withdraw their heavy weaponry from around Sarajevo so that a bombing like the one from the market could not reoccur. There was a stand off for a time. There were mediators involved, also from Russia. And one morning, quite early, and, as I recall, a Sunday morning, but I may be wrong about that, we were called. My -- the Belgrade bureau chief, my producer was called asking us to come to the Bosnian Serb Presidency and when we arrived there, a crew from BBC television were also there with their correspondent, John Simpson, and John and I thought that we had been asked to go there for an interview with Mr. Karadzic to react to what NATO was saying at the time. We were wrong. We were actually there because the highest military council of the Bosnian Serbs were meeting, and the Bosnian Serbs wanted Sky News and the BBC to film this, and so it was the cameraman and the producer from Sky and from the BBC who were taken into the room. Mr. Karadzic was there, a number of other generals. And John and I were left waiting in a hall or an anteroom. And then Mr. Mladic walked in surrounded by a number of other Bosnian Serb officers. Seeing me, he began, well, really shouting at me in Serbo-Croat, a language that I don't really understand, and he walked up to me and grabbed me in my face, like this, which made it impossible for me to answer even if I could have understood what he was saying. The only two words that I understood -- I mean, I got the general gist of what he was trying to say, that he did not think I was the world's greatest journalist, but there were two words he used specifically which I did understand which were the words, Zuc and the word Gorazde. Zuc is a hill on the north western side of Sarajevo that, in December 1992, it had been held by the Bosnian Serbs was taken by the Bosnian army, and the day after they captured it, I was taken by the Bosnian army to film on Zuc and did a report on the capture of Zuc by the Bosnian army. As far as I am aware, the Bosnian Serb leadership never admitted to the fall of Zuc. Gorazde, I take it, this was a city, an enclave in Eastern Bosnia, and I walked in -- in the beginning of 1993, in February 1993 through Serb lines and spent some two weeks in the besieged enclave, and I imagined that Mr. Mladic was expressing his displeasure with my reporting of the fall of Zuc and of me entering the besieged enclave of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you described, you said, just in your last answer, "Grabbed me in my face, like this," and you gestured and you grabbed the chin and cheek of your face with your hand.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that the way that Mr. Mladic grabbed your face?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- as I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you say anything to him after this encounter or during the course of the encounter?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, during the course of the encounter as he was holding me, I couldn't say anything at all. When he let go and walked away, the only thing I said was, I will see you in The Hague. John Simpson then said to me that that was rather a weak repost. But here we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no questions -- no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Groome. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to do this now or at a time later in the day, but there are ten associated exhibits that the Prosecution has not worked with but does intend to tender. Mr. Lukic has informed me that he would prefer to submit legal arguments after the witness finishes, so I will be guided by the Chamber, whether the Chamber would like me to place them on the record now or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe let's deal with them at a time when it is both convenient for both of you to talk about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll just start briefly with what you said today during your testimony. First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Lukic. I'm not hearing any translation -- I beg your pardon. Okay. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your abridged statement that was given to us by Mr. Groome, it says that you were commander of a mortar platoon. Were you a mortar platoon commander in actual fact, or were you trained to be one?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was trained to be an officer in the Royal Netherlands Marine Corps which is generally an infantry unit, and I was given specific training with mortars and was then was also, for a time, the commander of a -- of a mortar battalion in the Netherlands Antilles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And for how long were you a platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: For a year. I was doing my military service. Generally, in the Netherlands, that would have been 14 months, but the Dutch marine corps is nearly -- or was, in those days, nearly completely professional and if you wanted to do -- be a reserve officer, you had to serve for at least two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, I'm a bit confused because it was said that you were in Sarajevo from 1992 until 1995. Can you tell us now when was it that you actually were in Sarajevo? We know that you arrived at the end of May 1992. How long did you stay the first time? When did you leave? When did you come back? Because I think that this is inaccurate, to say that you were in Sarajevo all the time.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do not recall ever saying that I was in Sarajevo all the time. It's certainly inaccurate. If that is stated anywhere. I was in Sarajevo May/June, I left for a period in June of about a week and then returned and stayed there throughout July until early August. In September, I was in Pale as we've already seen, and I was again in Sarajevo throughout -- from late October until the middle of -- well, no, the 20th or 21st of December of that year. In the years that followed, I visited Sarajevo in 1993, in 1994, in 1995, and 1996. Usually I stayed shorter, and I spent more time in Central Bosnia and there were also periods when I was not in Bosnia at all, when I was sent to Moscow or to other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You showed us what it was that you could see from the military hospital and you say that you used it as a centre for filming. For example, from this hospital, you could not see Dobrinja; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is right. Dobrinja lies next to Sarajevo airport right in the western side of the city, and you could not see it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And today we saw that burning building, and we also heard the report that you made. When you were there, when the firing had already started, before it started, when were you there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The question is not completely clear to me in translation. We arrived, and some of those flats were already on fire. And the bullets were hitting that building. That continued after we arrived. We were driving from the city centre to Sarajevo television station at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that people told you that the building was not used by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But you didn't check that yourself, did you, those allegations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We checked as far as we could. What you look for is you look for any men in uniform. Certainly by December 1992 the Bosnian army had actually -- actually existed and was quite well organised. You looked for anything that could be a sign; for instance, spent casings from bullets because they didn't go around clearing those up. We asked the people living there, and then we went to the UN to ask them. They have rather more people around. We were just one small team. And they told us that it had not been used to the best of their knowledge by the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you actually enter the building?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That day?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you didn't record that? Or perhaps we didn't see that here today.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Whether I entered it with the cameraman or whether you entered it with my field producer, that I can't remember. Whether the cameramen came in, that is quite possible that we left him outside and that we went in. I should just add, it is something that we were aware of that we had to be careful of is to check as much as possible whether any target had been used by the military to make it a legitimate military target for their opponents. So it is something that we always checked on. Also, at the former military hospital when we first arrived there, certainly as we were going to be spending our nights there, it is something that I checked on as carefully as I could because if it had been used by the Bosnian military then we were obviously -- I was putting my own crew in greater danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In any case, you were not able to check the apartments that were burning, if the soldiers were there in these apartments that were shot at?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. This is not a police investigation in a city that is not at war when you have the freedom to do that kind of thing. This was a city at war, and, therefore, the investigation we did was absolutely limited by those constraints.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to go into more detail about the parliament. Today you said that the parliament was also -- the parliament building was also shot at. At the time, was the building being used as a parliament building or was somebody else occupying it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The parliament has its -- consisted of two buildings. A tower, let's say on the right from the pictures that we're using, and then a lower building on the left. I had actually been in the lower building on the left. This was a front line position, Your Honours, and we saw Bosnian soldiers in that lower building. I did not enter the higher building, so I am not aware if it was or was not used by the Bosnian military as well. But the lower building, absolutely was, yes. And it was not being used as a parliament at the time. I mean, there was a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said in paragraph 55 of your statement something about how the artillery should decide on a target and how it should concentrate its fire on that one target. Is this the regular procedure even if you have a thousand targets in one place? Would you also focus just on one in that case?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: One might well focus on more, but the kind of fire on each target would be sustained fire. Because otherwise it really, from a military point of view is nonsensical. You want to then destroy that target and just firing one shell at a target is not going to do that. Quite apart from that, one would have to be incredibly lucky if one were to hit the target with just one or two shells. As I've already described to the Court, this -- this takes time, and nearly always it takes more shells on one target and this is what we witnessed on the Marsal Tito barracks. It was in the end, not initially, that is normal in -- with the use of artillery. In the end it was accurate and sustained fire and it continued for a very long time; in fact, not just one night, but two. But most of the rest of the fire did not give me the indication that they were firing at 1.000 targets in a sustained manner that I would think would be normal for artillery to be used in in the manner that it had been explained to me by professional artillery officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will come to what they explained to you, and we will make comparisons between the US army and the US -- and the Bosnian army and we will also compare terrain in Sarajevo and Iraq. But now, I would like to go back to something and I will put this question which I think is not disputed. You said earlier today that you do not speak Serbo-Croatian, or B/C/S, as we call it in this Tribunal today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All the information that you got from conversations was information that you received through an interpreter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. There were conversations in English. Mr. Karadzic spoke English; Mr. Milosevic spoke English. One encountered other people who spoke English, doctors. Not usually within the Yugoslav Army. And then, yes, I would need a translator. This was usually my field producer, Zoran Kusevac, who did the translation for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at paragraph 12 of your statement, please. You say in this paragraph at the beginning: "It is impossible that the Bosnian Serb command, whether military or political, did not know what was happening in the Bosnian enclaves. I myself filed reports from the field about it, and my broadcasts were picked up by the local media." Which local media would broadcast Sky News?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I think I also said in my statement, initially when I first arrived in the former Yugoslavia, Sky News had a deal with Yugoslavia state television and we were broadcast, if I remember correctly, 12 hours a day on what was called the Third Channel. Later, this was stopped, but our reports were picked up and used without any asking of permission by anyone who wished. As far as I am aware, there were special programmes made both in Bosnia and in Croatia on the lines of what others are saying about us, and many of the reports that I filed, indeed even many of the lives I did when I'm questioned from the studio in London, they were rebroadcast by those television stations also, at times, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you don't know exactly when and which media in Republika Srpska? You're not able to tell us this now? So that we could check that, if you do know?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The reports -- or at least some of the reports that I did in September 1992 were used by the television station in Pale, and I discussed them with Mr. Karadzic and some of his advisors. They watched it there. Mr. Karadzic did quite a lot of lives into Sky as well. And Mr. Mladic much have watched as well because when we encountered him after the interview, he knew one of the lines that I had used, and he said that he'd seen the report and that he was not displeased with it. Some people in Pale were displeased with it, but he was personally not. That's why I say they could watch our reports, and we knew that they were watching our reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your reports were in English; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is correct. But they were translated by those media that then decided to rebroadcast them. Again, without any control on our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now could you please look at paragraph 18 of your statement. You say: "To my knowledge, Bosnian Serb forces held the high ground around the city in May at this time. At this stage, the airport was also in Serb hands." Let me ask you this first: Were there lines of separation at the time? Were the armies facing each other along the front lines?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure that in May 1992 you can actually speak of a Bosnian army. You can speak of various armed units, but of an army, not under the definition that I would use. There was clearly -- when we crossed from Ilidza to -- into Sarajevo, there was clearly a -- what I would call a no man's land between the front lines on the Bosnian Serb side and the front lines on the Bosnian side. It was a very dangerous things to do. One of the first rules of war for any war correspondent is don't cross lines. In Bosnia, we had to do this often and you often got shot at and you never knew who was shooting at you. There was clearly a front line there. There seemed to us at some of the locations that we were taken to, for instance, when we were taken to near the Jewish cemetery but then on the Bosnian side, that there was clearly a front line there too. But I didn't go everywhere in the city. The city was too big, than was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke a lot with Mr. Karadzic in 2010 about these hills that were occupied, and it turned out that actually at that time and today you don't know which army held which hill at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. We were actually told in Pale that the Bosnian Serbs were holding the high ground. And you go onto Mount Trebevic on your way to Sarajevo, and that's where the Bosnian Serb forces were throughout the war. At higher positions and at lower positions. As one drove into Grbavica, you would only encounter Bosnian Serb forces. When I was taken to Zuc, this hill had clearly been in possession of the Bosnian Serbs, and the military commander there pointed out ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the military commander there pointed out to the other positions around that and told me they were under control of the Bosnian Serbs. Another thing that was -- when I -- after my interview with Mr. Mladic in September 1992, we were taken by the two military policemen on a road that had been build specifically by the Bosnian Serb army, we were told, and this is on the northern to Vogosca, all the way -- we went all the way to Ilidza and even to the front near to Hadzici. And all the way we were told, These are positions held by us, and this was the northern high ground around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In any event, today, you are saying that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not hold positions at Trebevic at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, not on the main mountain side, no. I mean, and not on the road, if you come down that road, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The elevations closer to town. Do you know that they were held by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There were certain positions, let's say, in the south-east of Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, let's just stop here. We're talking about Trebevic. Are you also speaking about Trebevic or some other positions? Are you aware that the positions in Trebevic closer to town were held by the forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, I was never taken by them there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we can conclude that all the fire that came from Trebevic, that you ascribe that fire to the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, if it was hitting Sarajevo and the Bosnian part of Sarajevo held by the Bosnian forces, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 21 of your statement, you say: "People lived as much as they could in the basements of their apartments or in bomb shelters." Does that mean that the apartments were empty?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness's statement is in evidence as P66, and although all of us in the courtroom here have access to it, I wonder whether those viewing the trial would not be assisted by having it placed on e-court. So I would ask or suggest to the Chamber that perhaps the statement be placed on e-court and the appropriate paragraph be displayed there as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have no objection to this proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll do that. May the statement please be shown in e-court. Paragraph 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have that on our screens now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was: Were the apartments in Sarajevo empty, since, as you say -- or said at the time, people were living in basements or in bomb shelters?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, they were not. People would take to the bomb shelters, or to the basements and bomb shelters if they were lucky when there was heavy shelling. But, of course, people went up to their apartments for their clothes, for food to eat. And it depended on the period in Sarajevo. You had that period that I have described in court this morning of early June 1992 when people did spend a lot of time in -- in -- in shelters or basements, but there were other periods of time during the war in Sarajevo when they would not have done so and would have been in their apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the civilian buildings in Sarajevo were turned into military positions right from the beginning of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In an urban war, where there are front lines within the city, then obviously. What were prior civilian buildings or businesses are likely to find. If they are on the front lines, then they will definitely be turned into -- that is, I would say, obvious in any urban battle ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're referring only to buildings that are on the front line, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly on the front lines, Your Honour. But, of course, I'm also aware that certain other buildings that may previously have been businesses, generally I would think businesses, the ones that I saw, but I didn't see that many were turned into various kinds of headquarters of the armed forces. But, again, in a city under siege, that is almost bound to occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And can we now look at paragraph 22 of your statement, please. You said that: "The United Nations had to seek permission to be allowed access across front lines so that food and aid could be delivered to one's enemies. They had to ask permission from one side." Humanitarian aid did come into Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you know how much humanitarian aid came into Sarajevo on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We were told by the UNHCR that that varied. We were also told in December 1992 by one of the senior figures of UNHCR in Sarajevo that it was never enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume that in war time, no one has enough; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Oh, there are certain people in war time who have more than enough. There's always those who actually make money out of war. But what I will --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it's a vast minority of people who use the war in that way.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And, for me, one of the strange things about the war in Bosnia was that it was the first time that I'm aware of that the United Nations stepped in with a humanitarian relief programme and asked one side to stop shooting so that they could feed the enemies, and this did occur throughout the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the information that, other than ground convoys, there were about 10.000 humanitarian flights into Sarajevo during the period?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware that there were flights. The number I was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic. By "during the period," are you referring to the entire period of the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a war correspondent, did you know how much weaponry was coming into Sarajevo every day?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That would have been a wonderful scoop to get. But in any war, journalists are usually not privy to that information. The only war that I can recall where I was able to get some kinds of facts or figures was in the war in Afghanistan in the 1980s. But no military side in any war that have I been in, whether with militias, like in Beirut, for instance, in Lebanon, is going to give you that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 23, you talk about fuel. I'm not going to read here what you said. But I do want to ask you if you know what the situation was in the areas that were held by Serbs, as far as fuel is concerned?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: My experience - this is specifically Eastern Bosnia - was that people were using wood but wood that was more available, easily available from the forests where they lived rather than in a city like Sarajevo. But generally, as far as I'm aware, in places like Vlasenica or Pale, most people were using wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, but could you now answer my question. What was the situation with the parts of Sarajevo held by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Oh, I see, sorry. I thought you meant the Serbs -- the Bosnian Serbs. From my experience of what I saw there, specifically in September 1992, and again when I was taken into Grbavica in February 1994, the situation was that food was more plentiful than in the rest of Sarajevo but that there were also problems with that and that also there there was a problem with heating fuels.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the war, Sarajevo used gas for heating. It's Russian gas; do you know that? And do you know who turned that gas off? Who switches off gas when you don't pay your bill?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The provider, one imagines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The -- I was aware - because you asked me the question - that they used gas for heating. Some gas at certain moments was reinstated again during the war in Sarajevo. As to the situation between clients and customer on the gas front, I'm afraid that was not one of the things that I looked into carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next paragraph, 24, says that going out for water meant risking your life. Are you aware that on both sides of the separation line, UNPROFOR set up visual obstacles to hinder infantry fire directed at civilians?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm aware that on both sides of the separation line this was done. I never witnessed UNPROFOR actually doing this. I saw a lot of local initiatives. But I'm absolutely aware that this happened on both sides, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 25 of your statement you speak of a constant war of terror against the civilians. You say it was two-pronged in its approach: Shelling and sniper fire at civilians. In the course of these proceedings, we have already seen and we'll be seeing more about this, but I'm asking you: Do you know that the Muslims fired from sniper rifles at their own civilians in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I have never witnessed that. I have heard the allegations. I have never seen proof. And whether these were Muslims or simply members of the Bosnian army, you may take care in that, because within the Bosnian army, there were Muslims but there were also Catholics and Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many Serbs and Catholics were there in the ABH, in terms of percentages, if you know?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I couldn't give you percentages, but I found it noticeable that even when I went into the enclave of Bihac in late 1994, that's the commander of operations of the Bosnian army 5th Corps was a Serb, and that's the kind of situation that I did encounter elsewhere with other corps -- Bosnian army corps. But precise percentages, I couldn't give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the Karadzic trial, you were asked if you knew that in the Army of Republika Srpska there were whole units made up of Muslims. Since then, have you checked this, now that we're speaking of the national composition or ethnic composition of these two armies?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I haven't. But I would come to the question and ask: If this was the case, why were journalists like myself not taken to such units?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Regrettably you only get to answer questions, not ask them. Just as I only get to ask questions, not answer them.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I would just leave the question there for the Court to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My I interrupt you for a moment. You mentioned one Serb commanding in Bosnian Muslim army unit. Could you please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the commander of operations at the headquarters of the Bosnian army 5th Corps in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of this person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall the name of this person. I've met him but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I thought you would have mentioned his name but it was not recorded. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest, Your Honour, I have encountered more Serbs and Croats within the Bosnian army and it wasn't as if it was the exception that proved the rule, and therefore whilst I imagine somewhere in my notes I may have the name, it's 18 years ago. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The information we have is that Atif Dudakovic was the commander of the 5th Corps. He was a Muslim. It's just that he was a former JNA major and he was in the 220th Motorised Brigade. That is information that we have and that we will certainly debate further in the course of these proceedings, I expect. However --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I? I said he was the head of operations. That's G3. I didn't say he was the commanding officer of the Bosnian army 5th Corps. That is indeed Atif Dudakovic. We are talking about two different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we're talking about one person who remains anonymous for the time being, but we may be able to clarify it later. Let's come back to paragraph 25 of your statement regarding sniper positions. You visited a sniper position held by the Army of Republika Srpska, and we have seen that in your footage. Is it the case that you have never visited a sniper position held by the Bosnian Muslim forces in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We were taken in early June, as I've already mentioned, to positions held by the Bosnian army within part of the parliament building. I did not see any sniper rifles there. And at other locations along the front lines that I was allowed to go to, there may well have been snipers, but I did not see any sniping rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we have sat for an hour. If you can find a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Any moment is convenient for me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can we take it at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. May the witness please be escorted out of court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at the top of the hour. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be brought into court, please. And, Mr. Mladic, please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of course you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We established before the break that he have never visited the sniper positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, you cannot know today, nor were you able to know then, what these positions were facing and what they were targeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Sarajevo, did you learn how many civilians were killed in Sarajevo by armed Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Are you referring to people killed in Grbavica and the areas of Sarajevo held by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In areas held by Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In the area held by the Bosnian army, I was not given any figures by -- about how many people had been killed by their own side, is what you're trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. How many Serb civilians were killed in the territory of the city of Sarajevo held by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? In pure executions.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is not the question you originally asked. You asked about civilians, as I got the translation. And the answer is: I was not given those figures, no, if it happened; nor were we told, did we hear about such matters apart from when we were in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what did you hear in Pale?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: All sorts of conjecture, but not things that we were able to actually prove when we were on the ground inside Sarajevo; about prisons, about executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll come to a passage where you say -- where you describe how there were people on the ground in Sarajevo who were checking fire from Serb snipers in order to report whether somebody was hit or not. Do you know that pre-texts like that were used to enter Serb apartments, kill Serb civilians, to imprison people?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was not a witness to any such events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if you heard in Pale such allegations, such accusations, you did not deal with them when you were in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Incorrect. We absolutely asked. We tried to follow up also on certain occasions. There is one instance that I specifically recall in the period of November/December 1992 when we were in Sarajevo staying at the former military hospital that a Serb man was brought in wounded. We asked how he had been wounded. He had been wounded in his flat from fire from outside. We went to the flat, spoke to his wife, but we got -- the indications that we had, as far as we could work out, was that this fire had come from Bosnian Serb positions. I -- in the city, I was never told -- we asked but we never got any confirmation of the things that you are alleging right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am not alone in putting forward these facts. These facts will be proven amply during these proceedings. Was that the only time you inquired into the wounding of a Serb civilian in Sarajevo? And do you know the name of that civilian? Is it anywhere in your notes?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: What you prove or not prove has got nothing to do with me. You asked me a question, and I have given you an answer. Did we inquire into the wounding of people in Sarajevo whether they were Serb, Croat, or Muslim? Yes, we did. Could we always go somewhere? No, it's not always possible. But we did inquire. And we made inquiries about how -- if any of this was true at various levels. On the official level by going to the Bosnian Presidency, talking to people there, but also on a lower level talking to army units or police units about all of these things. We never found proof. We were never, maybe, put in that position, but we never could back up any of those allegations. As to your last question do I know the name of that civilian, well, I would have a really incredible memory if, 20 years later, I could pop out the name of one civilian. And the answer is I can't. Do I have it in my notes? I have no idea if I have it in my notes, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have your notes with you today?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Here?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In The Hague.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I have had to move back to The Hague with all of my possessions as I explained right at the beginning of today's hearing. I have not sorted out all my administration and all my notes from my various war zones, and therefore I don't know what I do or do no longer have. We moved a lot. My wife was a diplomate. Every three to four years, we moved from one city to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A similar question was put to you in May 2010 by Mr. Karadzic. You did not find it appropriate knowing that you would be testifying in this case to try to find your notes and see what's in them.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Shortly after I testified against Mr. Karadzic, my wife was -- got pancreatic cancer. I spent the rest of 2010 looking after her. We had to move back from Rome to Holland. When we were living in Rome, our belongings were still in the Netherlands, so immediately afterwards I could not look into my possessions. After my wife died, and I moved back from Rome to the Netherlands, all my possessions that had been locked up here did come back into my house, but, no, at that moment of my life, there were other things like trying to create a new life and get a job, to be quite frank with you, Mr. Lukic, that were more important to me than one notebook from one war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm truly sorry for what happened to you, and I offer you my sincere condolences of the death of your wife, but you will understand that we have to do our job, too, and there was no ill intent behind my question. At the trial of Mr. Karadzic on 19 May 2010, on page 2451 of the transcript, you spoke about your ability to verify certain information, primarily who was shooting at whom, where the fighting was going on, and you say at line 23: [In English] [Previous translation continues] "... with both sides as far as possible but often it was an impossibility. We simply didn't get answers." [Interpretation] Can we agree that you were aware that you were putting out unverified information?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In any war as a war correspondent it is fairly difficult when there is an engagement to call both sides and say, Could you please give me your version of what happened. Almost a ridiculous point to make. One tried as much as one could to verify, and to be as accurate as we possibly could be. That said, it is done at that time. You are in a war zone. You are yourself being shot at. And that -- not all information you give may be 100 percent accurate is also true. But then I have learnt in my life in war zones that the truth is a complex many-sided thing. I am aware of that, and we tried always in our reports to be as careful as possible, to be as accurate as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also on the same day, on page 2464, you say: [In English] [Previous translation continues] "... if we are not shown and if we are not told, how are we meant to know?" [Interpretation] That also fits into your previous answer, that you were trying to find out as much as you could, but it's possible that you did not always receive correct information and that would, consequently, lead to inaccurate reporting. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am concerned that the witness had just been given or read a portions of his answers. A little unfair to the witness and I would request that Mr. Lukic read the question and the answer so that the witness can fully appreciate the context of his answer. It is some time ago that he gave this evidence. I believe he should have the ability to understand, at least the question and the full answer that he gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately cut only this portion so if my learned friend from the other side have the question and the answer if front of him, I am glad to hear and the witness can hear both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that if the Court feels that's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the question before the answer or that -- or the portion of the answer that Mr. Lukic is -- the following quote: "Q. But, Mr. van Lynden, Ilijas is the location where most of the shells in this war fell and proportionally their losses were the great civilians and soldiers. Sarajevo municipality that totally -- that your interest did not focus on at all. "A. But, Mr. Karadzic, if that's the case, why were we not taken there by your government and by your army? If we are not shown and we are not told how are we meant to know? You cannot have correspondents in a war zone running around freely without two front lines. You didn't show us. How is the rest of the world to know. I was never taken there by your government or by your army."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. van Lynden, let's just clear up one thing. Ilijas, the area referred to here, is a part of Sarajevo controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The Army of the Republika Srpska didn't take me there. This is the point I was trying to make to Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've heard that. Let's just establish one thing. Ilijas was a part of Sarajevo controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is being asserted here that that was the most heavily bombed area in Sarajevo throughout the war. Did you have any knowledge about that? You say here that the authorities of Republika Srpska did not take you there and did not show that to you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It is asserted by Mr. Karadzic that that is the case. I haven't heard it asserted by anyone else or at least it hasn't been done so to me, nor in the meetings that I had, either with Mr. Karadzic or with anyone else from the Bosnian Serbs, were we told this information at that time or taken there. So I repeat the point that I made two years ago. If you're not taken there and you're not told, how are we meant to know? And you cannot have a situation as I tried to also make clear to Mr. Karadzic of war correspondents freely driving around along the front lines. No army would accept that. And, by the way, no sensible war correspondent would do so. It would be pretty dangerous in a foreign country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that you did not see this and did not report about that, for the reasons that you mentioned yourself, are you challenging it here today, namely, that Ilijas -- are you saying that Ilijas is a part of Sarajevo that was not heavily bombed throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying anything of the kind. I'm saying that we were not given that information during the war and, therefore, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, Mr. Karadzic asked you -- actually, we have to go back to all of these things that he asked you because we have a statement of yours that is practically identical for both trials. This is what he asked you. He asked you about something that had been claimed by General Rose. You said yourself that you received information from UNPROFOR, that you had only three men on your team. At that time UNPROFOR had a lot more information because they're an international organisation with a lot more manpower; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Has this got to do with General Rose or -- well, UNPROFOR had thousands of people. We are a television news team. The two are clearly different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll get to General Rose. Is it true that you sought information from UNPROFOR and, indeed, received information from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: UNPROFOR would give briefings, and UNPROFOR would be willing -- some -- some of the officers to -- if we went there and had questions, to give us answers. Sometimes they did. Sometimes they didn't. Sometimes they said they knew. Sometimes they said they didn't know and didn't have the information. So, yes, we would go to UNPROFOR because we felt that this was the outside force not allied to either of the forces fighting the war, and, therefore, that we were more likely to get an objective answer as to what had actually happened on the ground from them than they would from either of the conflicting parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said something interesting now; namely, that UNPROFOR was impartial. How much do you know about UNPROFOR impartiality?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We accepted that UNPROFOR was a United Nations force drawn from various countries around the world. Therefore, there are always bound to be certainly imperfections of a military and organisational nature but that was not, in principal, partial to the war. There may have been certain individuals within UNPROFOR who were less impartial. But, generally speaking, my contact with most of the officers - most of the officers - of UNPROFOR was that they were relatively impartial. They were not sent there by their governments, nor was that the agreement reached at the Security Council for them to be partial. They weren't sent to intervene militarily in the war in Bosnia. They were sent there primarily to facilitate the food aid that we have already discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously you are talking about 1992. This impartiality, did it change over the years? Ultimately, did this impartial party bomb one of the parties involved in the conflict? Is it not a fact that NATO conducted air-strikes at the behest of UNPROFOR? Against Serb positions, that is.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm aware of NATO doing so in defence of areas that had been called safe havens that came under attack by the Bosnian Serbs. As far as I'm aware, the first time that such air power was used was in April 1994 around Gorazde. There, the UN clearly felt that, having declared safe havens, they had to also take action to see to it that that haven remained safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Just a moment, please. Thank you. What is a save haven? Would that be an armed stronghold or a disarmed area? What is your view of that? I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, regardless of that, which side the UNPROFOR sided with in 1995, General Rose -- well, let's not bring in his book now. But on pages 69 and 70, and this was put to you by Mr. Karadzic as well on the 21st of May, 2010. So, this is what General Rose says: "Many journalists in Sarajevo supported the military option, either because this was felt to be morally right or to engage in some kind of holy war against the Serbs, or because images of war sell better than images of peace." This is what I'd like to ask you first: Did you know about this position taken by General Rose?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the Prosecution please have the transcript reference of the Karadzic examination so that we can follow along.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] 2631 is the page number; lines 9 through 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So were you familiar with this position of General Rose?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I'm not a particular friend of General Rose's, so he hasn't actually mentioned this to me personally. This is his personal opinion. He is allowed a personal opinion, but he hasn't talked to me about it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that the Murdoch information empire advocated war against the Serbs? Mr. Murdoch who owned Sky News, inter alia.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Murdoch does not own Sky News. Mr. Murdoch is a minority shareholder in Sky. He tried to buy it last year and failed. The Murdoch information empire doesn't work as a hierarchical institution. Neither Mr. Murdoch nor any of the executives within BSkyB ever told us what to day, what to think. That simply didn't happen. I have no idea what the views are of Mr. Murdoch or of his children or of, indeed, of the board of his various enterprises as to the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Before you arrived in Bosnia, we saw all the jobs you had and where you worked. Inter alia, you say that you were in Afghanistan, I think, in 1980, and that you reported about the fighting of the Mujahedin against the Russian forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I made four treks into Afghanistan in the 1980s, Your Honours. In 1981, 1982, 1985, 1989 with a group of the Mujahedin from Pakistan, each trek about three months, whilst the country was still occupied by what was then called the Soviet Union, rather than the Russians, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You had good connections with the Mujahedin at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: If you were going to be taken by a group, it was actually -- I mean, this is -- you are crossing an international boundary without a visa, you have to know the people you are going with, because, really, if you are going into a guerilla war, you are putting your life in their hands. I found a commander called Abdul Haq with whom I had often difficult but good relations, yes. We came from different cultures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, you had to establish initial contact with the Mujahedin. How did you manage that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure of the relevance to this Court, but what would I would do is I -- we -- I went to Peshawar in 1981 and then went to the varios resistance groups with -- that had offices in Peshawar, asking them if they had a field commander who was returning into Afghanistan, specifically for the Kabul area because I felt that I could -- Afghanistan is a large country. I had to do this on foot. And I felt I could be most effective in my analysis if I went with a commander from the Kabul area. That's how I met Abdul Haq, in one of those offices. We then had fairly length negotiations, and then he agreed to take me with him. I wasn't introduced is what I'm trying to say. I just went out there to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order for you to be accepted, was this initial contact for you managed by some foreign intelligence service, or are you claiming that -- or are you claiming that the Mujahedin would just take in a foreigner, just like that, and admit him into their own ranks?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I -- I can understand that from -- certainly the perspective of your -- the person you are defending, it is very hard to understand what the Afghans were like or their organisation was like 31 years ago. I can assure you that it was very badly organised, but quite open where their headquarter were in Peshawar, and as a foreign journalist, you could simply walk in and try to do what I did. I was absolutely not brought by anyone else, not even another journalist. There had been journalists before me and there were many journalists after me who did the same thing I did. In the context of the present day, this is unthinkable. Anyone trying now to go with the Taliban who is a western journalist would not be able to do so. But 31 years ago if Peshawar, the way I've described it was the way that it happened. And the idea that foreign intelligence was in any way involved is a ludicrous one, but maybe not coming from someone who was an officer in the Yugoslav army, because that was the kind of mindset they grew up with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you this because we all know, and it's a generally known fact, that the CIA had a major part in organising this Mujahedin resistance to the Soviet Union. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In 1981, when I first entered Afghanistan, yes, there were weapons coming via Pakistan to the various resistance groups. These came from various sources. The largest source at that time that we saw was China, specifically in the forms of mines. At no stage in my reporting in Afghanistan was there a moment when I thought, This is a movement that is organised from abroad. Yes, it is true that during the conflict, specifically from 1985 until 1989 when the Soviet Union withdrew from Afghanistan, the supply of weapons, specifically of anti-aircraft rockets, did increase. These were undoubtedly funded by the United States of America. But you really do not understand Afghanistan if you think that the CIA ran that war. They didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask -- interrupt here. Mr. Lukic, where are we going with all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because we have to connect the presence of Mujahedins in Bosnia, and we have the line of questions regarding them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, if we want to connect the presence of Mujahedin in Bosnia with what happened in Afghanistan, do we need to go through the entire war in Afghanistan or could we just say that the people who were in Bosnia who came from Afghanistan and they were Mujahedin. One sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I wanted to establish the connection of this gentleman with Mujahedins and whether he was any dealings with their influx into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any question that you asked him that relates to that point that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I didn't know what I would get from the gentleman so I had to ask him first, and then my questions would develop depending on what he answers to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we stay relevant to the case before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just going to ask you one more question in relation to Afghanistan and then we're going to leave that subject aside. In an open source on the Internet, I found something that links you to arms supplies to the Mujahedin. Did you have anything to do with providing the Mujahedin forces with weapons at the time when you were in Afghanistan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A reference that is a bit more specific than an open source on the Internet. That can be really anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you repeat that, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness can give a considered answer to that, he must have something more specific than information that's out somewhere in the Internet. I mean, there's all sorts of information out on the Internet, a large majority of which is unverified or actually false. I'm suggesting that Mr. Lukic, in order for that question to be fair, needs to be more specific about the reference so that the witness can recognise it or actually produce whatever it is that he found on the Internet that he wishes the witness to comment on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get that information. Obviously I don't have it with me. I'll move on, Your Honour. We'll move to paragraph 26 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mean, can I just actually answer the question. The answer is absolutely no. Absolutely none at all. Anyone who is a correspondent for more than a couple of months but -- and, in my case, I did it for 23 years, you cannot survive by dangling in that kind of business.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now paragraph 26, please. So we're no longer dealing with Afghanistan. You say that you never saw a person being wounded by sniper fire but you saw some civilians who were -- who died soon after they were hit by sniper fire. First of all, I'd like to ask you whether you know what the difference is in terms of ammunition between a sniper rifle and a regular, ordinary rifle? Is the ammunition used the same? The ammunition used by the Army of Republika Srpska? Or was it different. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, and as far as I recall, I saw in September 1992 several different rifles. I am not an expert on sniping. And, again, as far as I am aware, the calibre of a bullet is different. But I'm not an expert. I was not trained in this within the marine corps. And, to be honest, Your Honours, one of the things that you actually don't do as a war correspondent is go out specifically searching to go out with a sniper. And I can explain why. It happened to a colleague of mine in Beirut who went with a sniper, who wanted to do a story on the life of a sniper. And when they got to the point the sniper said, I have two people I can shoot. You choose. You put yourself in a morally impossible position. I heard this story right at the beginning of my career and therefore have never sought to go out with a sniper. In September 1992, we were taken to certain positions, and there happened to be people there holding sniping rifles, but we didn't specifically ask for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's time, I think, to call it a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Lukic. Thank you so much. Mr. van Lynden, we are not done with your testimony. I am sure you are aware of that. And let me just say what is abundantly obvious to you. While you are on the witness-stand, you may not discuss the case with anybody, least of all with the Prosecution now that you are under cross-examination already. You may stand down and come back tomorrow morning at 9.00. Same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Court will adjourn and come back at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of August, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
